scope: Five institutional research perspectives, not institutional participation

usss.label: Financial integrity
usss.summary: Trace documented payment risks without treating every commercial transaction as a war crime.
usss.boundary: No bank access, covert financial surveillance, criminal adjudication or export-control authority assumed.
usss.handoff: Public financial-exposure matrix, procedural-status summary, corrective compliance question.
usss.signal: Financial fraud or sanctions-evasion concern documented in a public administrative or court source.

sources.label: Secret Service Cyber Fraud Task Forces

chapters.title: Mission in one minute
chapters.plain: A public-interest researcher can study cyber-enabled financial crimes and payment-system integrity without acting as an investigator.
chapters.advanced: USSS Cyber Fraud Task Forces address defined financial and cyber-enabled offenses; public archive work is not a basis to access private banking or identity data.
chapters.practice: Write one sentence identifying the potentially relevant financial-crime behavior; state the legal question rather than asserting guilt.
chapters.acceptance: Can the described activity be distinguished from a lawful commercial payment?
chapters.avoid: Overstating jurisdiction from a sanctions or export allegation alone.

chapters.title: Understand the lawful boundary
chapters.plain: Financial integrity is the lens, not secret intelligence or war policy.
chapters.advanced: A payment involving Russia is not automatically fraudulent or forbidden. Distinguish payer, payee, beneficial owner, reason for payment, applicable sanctions, and evidence of concealment.
chapters.practice: Sketch a five-field public payment flow without private account identifiers.
chapters.acceptance: Is there an actual suspected financial offense and a competent referral authority?
chapters.avoid: Collecting bank account numbers, private addresses, or inferred criminal intent.

chapters.title: Build a dated source trail
chapters.plain: Start with public regulatory notices, court records and corporate statements.
chapters.advanced: Record publication date, period covered, exact conduct alleged, sanctions designation versus final conviction, and whether rebuttals exist.
chapters.practice: Add one dated government notice and one corroborating independent publication.
chapters.acceptance: Could another reviewer reproduce the conclusion from those sources?
chapters.avoid: Treating a sanctions listing as a criminal verdict.

chapters.title: Disambiguate corporate entities
chapters.plain: Check which legal entity appears in each document.
chapters.advanced: Match names against jurisdiction, registration, subsidiaries and ownership changes; do not collapse affiliates or similarly named firms into one legal person.
chapters.practice: Create manufacturer / exporter / intermediary / importer columns and mark missing links.
chapters.acceptance: Do corporate relationships come from documented filings rather than names alone?
chapters.avoid: Assigning all subsidiary conduct to a parent without evidence.

chapters.title: Construct a non-sensitive transaction timeline
chapters.plain: Sequence publicly documented events before drawing causation.
chapters.advanced: Separate contract date, export date, payment date, delivery and enforcement action; record uncertainty when only ranges are available.
chapters.practice: Draw a three-event timeline from a court filing or regulation.
chapters.acceptance: Can each date be traced to its source and timezone where material?
chapters.avoid: Inventing unknown payment pathways.

chapters.title: Identify evidence of knowledge
chapters.plain: Knowledge is a separate legal and factual question.
chapters.advanced: Look for adjudicated admissions, falsified end-user certificates, evasive routing described in filings and court-tested communications, while tracking exculpatory evidence.
chapters.practice: Classify two examples as allegation, official administrative finding or adjudicated criminal fact.
chapters.acceptance: Does cited evidence establish knowing conduct or merely financial proximity?
chapters.avoid: Assuming that discovering a component proves manufacturer complicity.

chapters.title: Choose the appropriate authority
chapters.plain: Referral ownership depends on the activity and law.
chapters.advanced: A financial-fraud concern may involve USSS and prosecutors; export licensing/enforcement generally implicates BIS, HSI or other competent agencies. Coordinate only through existing lawful channels.
chapters.practice: Draft a short public-source routing table with two possible recipient types.
chapters.acceptance: Have you avoided claiming that a public-interest prototype can submit a government case?
chapters.avoid: Presenting an unofficial project as a Secret Service task force.

chapters.title: Design a proportional safeguard
chapters.plain: Protect lawful commerce and innocent parties.
chapters.advanced: Recommend distributor due diligence, payment-screening quality assurance and record retention before sweeping payment restrictions; ask counsel about legal bases and exceptions.
chapters.practice: Draft one bounded intervention with civilian cost, reversal trigger and independent outcome.
chapters.acceptance: Would a false positive freeze legitimate humanitarian or civilian funds?
chapters.avoid: Financial exclusion without authority or due process.

chapters.title: Collaborate without leaking data
chapters.plain: Share only the minimum public facts required for independent review.
chapters.advanced: Use recipient-specific public-only JSON with source URLs, confidence, limitations and an explicit absence of agency endorsement. No personal identifiers, covert communications or live institutional link.
chapters.practice: Prepare a hypothetical public-only handoff and inspect each field.
chapters.acceptance: Can the receiver evaluate the issue without sensitive facts?
chapters.avoid: Auto-sharing local or peer data because Trystero is connected.

chapters.title: Measure outcomes and review errors
chapters.plain: A better metric is lawful, documented correction—not the number of accusations.
chapters.advanced: Track verified filing corrections, screened transactions reviewed by authorized compliance teams, substantiated referrals and false-positive reversals.
chapters.practice: Write a metric, one warning trigger and a stop rule.
chapters.acceptance: Would measurement reward accuracy and civilian safety rather than volume?
chapters.avoid: Treating a proposal as successful enforcement.

fbi.label: Lawful case evidence
fbi.summary: Keep legal proceedings, manufacturer origin, exporter identity and proof of knowledge separate.
fbi.boundary: No investigations, suspect surveillance, private data collection or purported official referrals.
fbi.handoff: Public-source case chronology, proof ladder, correction and alternative explanation.
fbi.signal: A public court record or enforceable export-control question exists.

chapters.title: What the FBI does
chapters.plain: The FBI has investigative and intelligence functions under law; this community system has neither.
chapters.advanced: Relevant public lenses include transnational procurement conspiracies, economic espionage, cyber incidents and federal criminal process. Roles overlap with DOJ, Commerce BIS and HSI.
chapters.practice: Choose one public case and identify exactly what law and institution it involved.
chapters.acceptance: Are you describing public education rather than opening a private investigation?
chapters.avoid: Confusing a research index with a law-enforcement case system.

chapters.title: Legal stage and presumption
chapters.plain: A charge is not a conviction.
chapters.advanced: Distinguish complaint, indictment, guilty plea, verdict, sentencing and administrative sanctions. State what is known about the evidentiary burden in each source.
chapters.practice: Mark three casebook claims by procedural posture.
chapters.acceptance: Can a defendant rebuttal or subsequent outcome change the phrasing?
chapters.avoid: Identifying someone as guilty based solely on an allegation.

chapters.title: Component origin versus end use
chapters.plain: Manufacturer origin and knowing illicit export are different claims.
chapters.advanced: Use manufacturer identity, product model, export documentation, consignee and unit-level provenance separately; never convert same-model shipment into serial-level proof.
chapters.practice: Build a five-link evidence chain and leave unidentified links explicitly blank.
chapters.acceptance: Which links are documented versus inferred?
chapters.avoid: Equating product origin with knowledge of prohibited transfers.

chapters.title: Open-source case chronology
chapters.plain: Public dockets and press releases require context.
chapters.advanced: Record charged time period, alleged mechanism, jurisdiction, cooperating agencies and stated limits; dates of publication may postdate the conduct.
chapters.practice: Create a citation-first chronology with one counter-source or defense statement.
chapters.acceptance: Could a reviewer distinguish the crime date from the reporting date?
chapters.avoid: Cherry-picking prosecutors’ allegations as adjudicated facts.

chapters.title: Export control crosswalk
chapters.plain: Not all suspected technology diversion belongs to the FBI alone.
chapters.advanced: BIS administers export controls; criminal investigations and prosecutions can involve FBI, HSI, DOJ and other partners. Any concrete compliance action requires professional legal review.
chapters.practice: Write a hypothetical handoff with separate control, investigation and prosecution owners.
chapters.acceptance: Does the action rest within the identified authority?
chapters.avoid: Conflating regulatory enforcement, national intelligence and civilian policing.

chapters.title: Protect evidence integrity
chapters.plain: Preservation and authenticity are separate from guilt.
chapters.advanced: Use original URLs, archived date, file SHA-256 and preservation notes. Hashes establish file consistency, not truth, authorship or chain of custody by themselves.
chapters.practice: Hash an authorized local public document and record context.
chapters.acceptance: Do you know who obtained the material and when?
chapters.avoid: Handling stolen, classified, or private evidence inside a public peer room.

chapters.title: Cyber incident boundaries
chapters.plain: Support reporting and defense only.
chapters.advanced: Public guidance can address secure backups, access control, phishing resilience and documenting observable harm. Do not probe targets, intercept traffic or trace private individuals.
chapters.practice: Develop a lawful defensive incident checklist for a public institution.
chapters.acceptance: Are all recommended measures defensive and consent-based?
chapters.avoid: Turning an incident review into intrusion or surveillance instructions.

chapters.title: Minimize privacy harms
chapters.plain: Better evidence should not require more unnecessary personal data.
chapters.advanced: Remove names of private persons, banking details, unneeded device identifiers and exact civilian whereabouts. Public court names still deserve contextual, non-defamatory treatment.
chapters.practice: Redact a sample public handoff and note justified inclusions.
chapters.acceptance: Could the same analytical result be achieved with less data?
chapters.avoid: Publishing witness information or sensitive personal addresses.

chapters.title: Referrals and reciprocal review
chapters.plain: Propose routing; never simulate official submission.
chapters.advanced: Offer a concise public-source memo with issue, sources, legal-status classification, limitations, competent authorities and steps requiring authorized investigators.
chapters.practice: Prepare a two-paragraph public referral draft for independent professional review.
chapters.acceptance: Does the draft clearly state it was not sent?
chapters.avoid: Faking agency credentials or confirmation.

chapters.title: Correct, withdraw, and audit
chapters.plain: A corrected record is evidence of quality.
chapters.advanced: Track challenges, source corrections, acquittals, withdrawn allegations and record retractions. Disclose when a prior inference must change.
chapters.practice: Revise one hypothetical mistaken claim and keep its correction history.
chapters.acceptance: Can the system reverse a harmful assertion quickly and transparently?
chapters.avoid: Preserving erroneous accusations for gamified XP.

cia.label: Competing foreign explanations
cia.summary: Explore alternative hypotheses, confidence, source gaps and diplomatic implications.
cia.boundary: No clandestine collection, foreign influence operations, covert action or policy authority.
cia.handoff: Dated analytic note, competing hypotheses, disconfirming evidence and confidence rationale.
cia.signal: Multiple plausible explanations materially affect a civilian-safe recommendation.

sources.label: CIA: foreign intelligence and no police authority

chapters.title: Foreign analysis, not law enforcement
chapters.plain: This module models disciplined foreign-source analysis. It is not the CIA or a covert tool.
chapters.advanced: CIA produces foreign-intelligence analysis for decision-makers and does not itself make policy. No collection tradecraft, clandestine methods or domestic enforcement are provided.
chapters.practice: Describe a foreign-policy question in neutral, answerable terms.
chapters.acceptance: Have you avoided speaking as though the system is an official agency?
chapters.avoid: Using analysis claims to justify covert action.

chapters.title: Define the question and baseline
chapters.plain: A precise question prevents vague speculation.
chapters.advanced: Specify geography, period, actors, known facts, assumptions and how the answer could change a lawful civilian-protection or diplomacy decision.
chapters.practice: Rewrite “Why does war continue?” into a narrowly testable observation question.
chapters.acceptance: What dated evidence would answer it?
chapters.avoid: Treating broad narratives as evidence.

chapters.title: Separate source types
chapters.plain: A statement by a party is a fact about what was said, not proof the claim is true.
chapters.advanced: Tag VERIFIED RECORD, PARTY CLAIM, INFERENCE, LEGAL FINDING and UNKNOWN; distinguish official institutional views from independently corroborated observations.
chapters.practice: Grade three claims and write one sentence of uncertainty for each.
chapters.acceptance: Can the label be justified without relying on author reputation alone?
chapters.avoid: Conflating government position with objective fact.

chapters.title: Competing hypotheses
chapters.plain: Never stop at the first plausible explanation.
chapters.advanced: Construct at least two causal models—security dilemma, territorial ambitions, economic constraints, political incentives—and list discriminating signals and inconvenient facts for each.
chapters.practice: Write two models of a stalled negotiation and one falsifier per model.
chapters.acceptance: Would the second model change your recommendation if verified?
chapters.avoid: Inventing hidden motives or confidential intelligence.

chapters.title: Timeline and base rates
chapters.plain: Temporal order does not automatically imply causation.
chapters.advanced: Mark when assistance, attacks and announcements occurred; test whether changes preceded claimed effects and what alternative drivers exist. Do not invent event probabilities.
chapters.practice: Build a before/after timeline and list confounders.
chapters.acceptance: Can the analysis distinguish coincidence from an observed mechanism?
chapters.avoid: Presenting correlation as intention.

chapters.title: Confidence calibration
chapters.plain: Explain why confidence is limited.
chapters.advanced: Confidence should reflect independent corroboration, source proximity, alternative explanations and evidence gaps—not an arbitrary numeric probability.
chapters.practice: Write a high/medium/low confidence note with reasons and future tests.
chapters.acceptance: Is the confidence label consistent with the evidence?
chapters.avoid: Showing spurious “93% certainty” for political intentions.

chapters.title: Early warning with stop rules
chapters.plain: Focus on observable civilian-risk indicators.
chapters.advanced: Look for public infrastructure incident records, humanitarian access changes, negotiation declarations and verifiable compliance. Avoid location-specific targeting or real-time combat intelligence.
chapters.practice: Choose three non-operational early-warning indicators and reporting cadence.
chapters.acceptance: Would reporting reveal protected civilian movements or humanitarian vulnerabilities?
chapters.avoid: Publishing sensitive operational location information.

chapters.title: Structured dissent
chapters.plain: Dissent strengthens a finding when grounded in evidence.
chapters.advanced: Write strongest alternative interpretation, its supporting source, and a clear observation that could reverse the finding. Encourage corrections even when a team agreed.
chapters.practice: Author one analytic dissent memo of 150 words.
chapters.acceptance: Could a reader understand why credible people disagree?
chapters.avoid: Rewarding confidence or consensus instead of corrections.

chapters.title: Bridge foreign analysis to diplomacy
chapters.plain: Assessment does not authorize negotiation.
chapters.advanced: Translate findings into conditional policy options for authorized decision-makers: action, independent verification, reciprocal response and civilian safeguard; mark decisions as external.
chapters.practice: Create three non-coercive diplomatic policy options with reversible steps.
chapters.acceptance: Does the summary preserve Ukraine’s sovereignty and negotiating agency?
chapters.avoid: Suggesting secret bargains made by the prototype.

chapters.title: Review and expiration
chapters.plain: Every finding should have an “expires when” rule.
chapters.advanced: Attach an as-of date and update triggers, archive obsolete assumptions and track what changed. Reassess after talks, new casualty data or substantiated contradictory records.
chapters.practice: Draft a correction trigger for one analysis.
chapters.acceptance: Could someone distinguish old analysis from current verified status?
chapters.avoid: Treating October 2026 material as perpetually live.

usmc.label: Civilian protection
usmc.summary: Review defense policy, harm prevention, non-operational ceasefire safeguards and recovery.
usmc.boundary: No military command, target selection, weapons employment, troop movements or offensive cyber.
usmc.handoff: Civilian-harm review, protective contingency, monitored compliance requirement.
usmc.signal: A proposed intervention may affect civilian safety or military escalation.

sources.label: DoD civilian harm mitigation action plan

chapters.title: Policy lens and legal remit
chapters.plain: This is a civilian-protection learning lens, not military command software.
chapters.advanced: Study U.S. defense-policy records, lawful security assistance, end-use accountability and DoD civilian-harm standards. It cannot issue orders or military recommendations for strikes.
chapters.practice: Summarize a published civilian-harm policy in ordinary language.
chapters.acceptance: Does the output avoid tactical targeting or weapons instructions?
chapters.avoid: Claiming the prototype controls U.S. forces.

chapters.title: Distinguish defense from aggression
chapters.plain: Weapons supply and war prolongation are not synonymous.
chapters.advanced: Separate lawful support for self-defense from illegal attacks and knowing facilitation of violations. Evaluate transfer conditions, recipient, end-use and observed behavior, not assumed motive.
chapters.practice: Build a two-column legal-purpose and observed-end-use table.
chapters.acceptance: What primary evidence supports each conclusion?
chapters.avoid: Treating all defense assistance as deliberate escalation.

chapters.title: Civilian harm assessment
chapters.plain: Start with people, not equipment.
chapters.advanced: Use public reports of deaths, injuries and damage; respect reporting gaps and avoid locations that expose civilians. Assess accessible shelter, health, water and energy effects.
chapters.practice: Choose a public harm metric and describe undercount risk.
chapters.acceptance: Can it be measured without identifying vulnerable people?
chapters.avoid: Using real-time strike data or protected coordinates.

chapters.title: End-use and procurement assurance
chapters.plain: Legitimate procurement can still require accountability.
chapters.advanced: Record contracting authority, export permission, intended use, monitoring provisions and civilian safeguards. A public researcher can propose audit questions but cannot conduct classified inspections.
chapters.practice: Write a lawful procurement-accountability checklist with missing-data fields.
chapters.acceptance: Have parties’ independent legal responsibilities remained distinct?
chapters.avoid: Publishing sensitive procurement routes.

chapters.title: Critical infrastructure resilience
chapters.plain: Emphasize defensive continuity planning.
chapters.advanced: Plan backup power, water continuity, medical supply redundancy and disaster recovery at non-sensitive planning levels. Favor civilian-led needs assessments.
chapters.practice: Outline a city-level service-resilience concept without exposing facility vulnerabilities.
chapters.acceptance: Can the same result be achieved without identifying targets?
chapters.avoid: Detailed weak-point mapping of critical systems.

chapters.title: Limited ceasefires and safety
chapters.plain: A ceasefire proposal needs consent and independent checks.
chapters.advanced: Define humanitarian scope, civilian-protection objective, incident reporting, independent adjudication and remedies, without supplying operational battlefield deployment details.
chapters.practice: Draft a non-operational energy-infrastructure truce checklist.
chapters.acceptance: What happens if one incident is disputed?
chapters.avoid: Treating an announced truce as implemented.

chapters.title: Incident evidence separation
chapters.plain: Observation is not a final legal finding.
chapters.advanced: Classify reported civilian harm, authenticated imagery, party claims, legal review and independent monitoring separately. Protect witnesses and avoid public chains that identify survivors.
chapters.practice: Mark three hypothetical incident records as confirmed, claimed or unresolved.
chapters.acceptance: Would protected persons be at risk if this record became public?
chapters.avoid: Publishing personally identifiable witness information.

chapters.title: Escalation premortem
chapters.plain: Design bounded-downside interventions.
chapters.advanced: Review whether monitoring signals can be spoofed, ceasefire provisions exploited, civilian relief politicized or third parties misunderstood; define a withdrawal trigger.
chapters.practice: Write a 24-month failure story then revise one safeguard.
chapters.acceptance: Would the fallback protect civilians if consensus collapses?
chapters.avoid: Optimizing military outcomes over protection.

chapters.title: Institutional handoff limits
chapters.plain: No single institution owns all pieces of peace.
chapters.advanced: Differentiate DoD civilian harm policy, DOJ enforcement, UN humanitarian mandates, independent civil society and Ukrainian consent; avoid informal transfers of sensitive data.
chapters.practice: Draw a public responsibility matrix with consent gates.
chapters.acceptance: Is every proposed recipient legally and practically appropriate?
chapters.avoid: Equating a research comparison with military coordination.

chapters.title: Reconstruction and recovery
chapters.plain: Durability means functioning services after hostilities.
chapters.advanced: Pair civilian resilience with local governance, technical standards, maintenance financing, independent audits and equitable access to benefits.
chapters.practice: Draft a recovery outcome metric and an independent audit step.
chapters.acceptance: Will benefits remain after donor funding ends?
chapters.avoid: Civilian dependency and unmeasured environmental harm.

un.label: Humanitarian assurance
un.summary: Center civilian needs, legal mandates, consent, impartial monitoring and durable recovery.
un.boundary: No automatic UN mission deployment, mandate, negotiation or access to protected humanitarian data.
un.handoff: Needs-based safeguard, consent/mandate gate, anonymized outcome metric.
un.signal: Civilians, protected populations, negotiations or international humanitarian norms are affected.

chapters.title: UN ecosystem, not one office
chapters.plain: The UN includes distinct bodies and mandates.
chapters.advanced: Differentiate OHCHR human-rights monitoring, OCHA humanitarian coordination, UNDP development, UNICEF child protection, Security Council mandates and peacekeeping missions.
chapters.practice: Match a proposed civilian need to an appropriate UN function.
chapters.acceptance: Is the specific body named rather than “the UN” as a monolith?
chapters.avoid: Pretending the project can dispatch a UN mission.

chapters.title: Charter principles and sovereignty
chapters.plain: Peace work begins with law and consent.
chapters.advanced: Respect the UN Charter, sovereignty, territorial integrity, human rights and international humanitarian law; distinguish de facto control from de jure recognition.
chapters.practice: Write the governing legal principle and note contested interpretations.
chapters.acceptance: Does a proposal avoid forced transfers or coerced territorial recognition?
chapters.avoid: False moral equivalence about invasion and lawful defense.

chapters.title: Humanitarian independence
chapters.plain: Aid must serve people, not bargaining leverage.
chapters.advanced: Apply humanity, neutrality, impartiality and operational independence appropriate to humanitarian actors. Do not make essential assistance conditional on political concessions.
chapters.practice: Design a needs-based distribution safeguard.
chapters.acceptance: Can relief reach civilians without exposing recipients?
chapters.avoid: Turning beneficiary records into intelligence or leverage.

chapters.title: Civilian casualty evidence
chapters.plain: Document harm with dates and uncertainty.
chapters.advanced: Use OHCHR reports and clearly separate verified minimum figures from alleged or likely larger totals; protect survivors, locations and witness identity.
chapters.practice: Write an accurately dated casualty indicator and its limitations.
chapters.acceptance: Could the number be safely audited and updated?
chapters.avoid: Treating unverified claims as total verified casualties.

chapters.title: Negotiation readiness
chapters.plain: Consent-dependent actions cannot be initiated by an app.
chapters.advanced: Clarify who can consent, who can monitor, which issues can be decoupled, and what the legal mandate would cover; protect Ukrainian agency and civilian participants.
chapters.practice: Make a consent checklist for a humanitarian access arrangement.
chapters.acceptance: Is it a proposal, a party claim or a signed and operating agreement?
chapters.avoid: Claiming a peace agreement exists from an announcement.

chapters.title: Monitoring mission authority
chapters.plain: UN peacekeeping requires authorization and practical consent.
chapters.advanced: Traditional principles include consent, impartiality and non-use of force except self-defense and defense of mandate. Security Council authorization, deployment and host acceptance cannot be assumed.
chapters.practice: Map what would have to be formally authorized for observers.
chapters.acceptance: Would this proposal still work if UN approval is blocked?
chapters.avoid: Presenting a “UN force” as already active.

chapters.title: Ceasefire incident reporting
chapters.plain: Use a neutral, protective reporting standard.
chapters.advanced: Define what counts as a report, minimum evidence, incident timestamp, independent reviewer, disputed status, safe disclosure and correction window.
chapters.practice: Create a fictional incident form without coordinates or protected identities.
chapters.acceptance: Can the parties contest a report through due process?
chapters.avoid: Posting raw testimony publicly.

chapters.title: POWs, missing people and children
chapters.plain: Humanitarian cases require confidentiality and specialized mandates.
chapters.advanced: Protect family privacy and use recognized humanitarian channels for tracing, detention and return issues. No crowdsourced person-tracking or location posting.
chapters.practice: Propose anonymized aggregate progress indicators.
chapters.acceptance: Are sensitive records kept out of peer rooms and public JSON?
chapters.avoid: Exposing detainees, children, or displaced families.

chapters.title: Recovery and reparations
chapters.plain: Durable peace needs community agency.
chapters.advanced: Prioritize water, health, shelter, education, demining and locally accountable procurement; separate needs estimates from funds committed, disbursed and spent.
chapters.practice: Draft a locally governed reconstruction monitoring concept.
chapters.acceptance: What independent community feedback can be measured?
chapters.avoid: Large donor-led plans without local consent or maintenance.

chapters.title: Peace durability and dissent
chapters.plain: A truce is not the same as a durable settlement.
chapters.advanced: Evaluate independent verification, compliance remedies, justice pathways, security commitments and survivor trust; preserve disagreement without abandoning fact standards.
chapters.practice: Compare a sectoral truce and a general armistice across five gates.
chapters.acceptance: Does the design survive a political or funding shock?
chapters.avoid: Declaring success solely because fighting paused briefly.

scenarios.title: Protect civilian services
scenarios.description: Keep water, health, food and energy service access measurable without identifying vulnerable facilities.
scenarios.deliverable: Public harm metric; community consent; independent reporting; stop if disclosure increases risk.

scenarios.title: Document restricted component diversion
scenarios.description: Separate manufacturer, exporter, intermediary and knowledge of unlawful transfer.
scenarios.evidence_source: Court records; corporate filings; BIS guidance
scenarios.deliverable: Five-link evidence chain; legal posture; non-accusatory public notice; corrected false positives.

scenarios.title: Assess a proposed sectoral ceasefire
scenarios.description: Test whether an energy or humanitarian pause has consent, defined scope, monitors and remedies.
scenarios.evidence_source: Party statements and independent observer reports
scenarios.deliverable: Consent matrix; public verified-incident aggregate; dispute mechanism; fallback.

scenarios.title: Map energy revenue and civilian costs
scenarios.description: Evaluate commercial trade links alongside legal relief exemptions and civilian effects.
scenarios.evidence_source: Independent energy trade research; official sanctions
scenarios.deliverable: Transaction categories; confidence notes; civilian cost; legal review.

scenarios.title: Defend civilian digital continuity
scenarios.description: Develop consent-based cyber resilience for relief organizations and public-service providers.
scenarios.evidence_source: Public defensive guidance and incident reports
scenarios.deliverable: Offline backup plan; incident-notification tree; no offensive probing.

scenarios.title: Rebuild services with community governance
scenarios.description: Compare sustainable recovery options and independent outcomes over years.
scenarios.evidence_source: World Bank, UN, public procurement reporting
scenarios.deliverable: Local ownership; lifecycle costs; audits; equity safeguards.

scenarios.title: Protect POW and missing-person processes
scenarios.description: Safely track aggregate humanitarian progress while keeping family records private.
scenarios.deliverable: Aggregate indicator; confidentiality review; no crowdsourced person tracking.

scenarios.title: Test competing narratives fairly
scenarios.description: Identify which claims are independently supported and which would change the conclusions.
scenarios.evidence_source: Court records, UN records and primary public statements
scenarios.deliverable: Two hypotheses; source matrix; corrections; protected identities.

scenarios.title: Improve public financial transparency
scenarios.description: Target verifiable illicit behavior without penalizing lawful aid or commerce.
scenarios.deliverable: Evidence-graded compliance memo; humanitarian exemption test; stop rule.

scenarios.title: Red-team a 24-month peace failure
scenarios.description: Challenge plausible agreements for noncompliance, spoilers, rearmament and civilian harm.
scenarios.deliverable: Failure story; independent metric; reversal trigger; protection fallback.

shared_gates: What is verified, alleged and missing
Proportional stop rule and safe fallback
